title: Development of a Machine Learning-Based Tool for Predicting Operative Time in Robot-Assisted Laparoscopic Hysterectomy.
journal: The Tohoku journal of experimental medicine

title: Subthalamic nucleus beta oscillations and sleep disorders in Parkinson's disease: A new perspective on deep brain stimulation regulation mechanisms and circuits.
abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is increasingly recognized as a multisystem neurodegenerative disorder that extends far beyond its classical motor manifestations. Among its non-motor symptoms, sleep disturbances are among the most prevalent and disabling clinical features, affecting up to 80% of patients and often preceding the onset of motor symptoms by several years. Recent electrophysiological studies have identified the subthalamic nucleus (STN) as a critical hub linking motor dysfunction to sleep abnormalities. Aberrant synchronization of beta (13-30 Hz) oscillations in STN local field potentials (LFPs) persists across wakefulness and sleep, disrupting normal sleep microarchitecture by suppressing slow-wave activity, impairing sleep spindle generation, and destabilizing sleep-stage transitions. These pathological beta oscillations have therefore emerged as a key electrophysiological hallmark of PD-associated sleep dysfunction. Subthalamic deep brain stimulation (STN-DBS), the current standard surgical treatment for advanced PD, has demonstrated significant benefits beyond motor symptom control. Accumulating evidence suggests that STN-DBS improves sleep through multiple complementary mechanisms, including suppression of pathological beta synchronization, restoration of cortico-basal ganglia-thalamocortical network dynamics, modulation of brainstem arousal circuits and neurotransmitter systems, and alleviation of nocturnal motor symptoms. This review summarizes recent advances in the neuroanatomical, electrophysiological, and circuit-level mechanisms linking STN dysfunction to sleep disorders in PD. We further discuss emerging therapeutic strategies and highlight future directions toward biomarker-guided, individualized treatment. Collectively, this review proposes a mechanistic framework linking STN electrophysiology to sleep regulation and identifies testable hypotheses that may facilitate the development of precision neuromodulation strategies for sleep disorders in Parkinson's disease.

title: Interpersonal neural synchrony: one label, many phenomena.
abstract: Brains synchronize interpersonally during social interaction, yet the term 'synchrony' is often used to describe phenomena with different origins and functional implications. In this article, we briefly synthesize and organize these phenomena according to their signal and coupling properties, highlighting the value of disambiguation for reproducibility, theoretical clarity, and translational impact.

title: On the nature of GABAB receptors and their plasticity in the mammalian brain.
abstract: Gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) is the principal inhibitory neurotransmitter of the mammalian CNS, essential for circuit function and behaviour. In the brain, GABA activates GABAA and GABAB receptors to modulate circuit activity on behaviourally relevant timescales. GABAB receptor signalling in pre- and postsynaptic domains of neurons is often overlooked, despite the strong inhibition it produces. Importantly, GABAB receptors are diversely phosphorylated and interact with various auxiliary subunits to modify function. This review compares the evidence for the expression and modulation of GABAB receptors, their effectors, and regulatory mechanisms between cell types, brain areas, and mammalian species, particularly focusing on the plasticity of these mechanisms and their relationship to neurological diseases such as epilepsy and dementia.

title: Predictors of early unfavorable outcomes in low NIHSS stroke patients undergoing thrombectomy: A case-control analysis of the Canadian OPTIMISE registry.
abstract: The benefit of endovascular thrombectomy (EVT) for patients with large vessel occlusion (LVO) stroke and National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS) ≤5 remains uncertain. Despite their initially mild presentations, many experience early deterioration and poor long-term outcomes. However, EVT carries procedural risks. We aimed to determine the prevalence of early unfavorable outcomes in EVT-treated low NIHSS patients and identify modifiable predictors. We conducted a retrospective case-control study using the Canadian OPTIMISE registry which captured EVT data nationwide (2018-2021). Adult patients with LVO stroke and admission NIHSS ≤5 treated with EVT were included. The primary endpoint, "early unfavorable outcome," was a composite of early neurological deterioration (NIHSS increase ≥4 within 24 h), symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage, in-hospital death, or discharge to long-term care. Cases were all patients meeting this endpoint; controls were matched 4:1 by age, sex, and baseline NIHSS. Modifiable predictors were analyzed using multivariable conditional logistic regression. Among 439 EVT-treated low NIHSS stroke patients, 50 (11%) experienced early unfavorable outcomes and were matched to 200 controls without unfavorable outcome. Unsuccessful reperfusion (TICI <2b) was the only modifiable factor significantly associated with early unfavorable outcomes (aOR 41.52, 95% CI 5.31-324.62, p<0.001). Prior IV thrombolysis, thrombectomy technique, and procedural complications were not associated. About one in ten EVT-treated low NIHSS patients experienced early unfavorable outcomes. Unsuccessful reperfusion was the strongest determinant. While reperfusion success is multifactorial and not entirely modifiable, this finding suggests that additional efforts to achieve complete recanalization in selected patients can be considered in appropriately selected patients. These findings provide real-world multicenter evidence pending the completion of ongoing randomized trials evaluating EVT in low NIHSS stroke.

title: Gustatory Connectivity and Central Projections of the Mouse Petrosal-Nodose-Jugular Ganglia Complex.
abstract: The petrosal, nodose, and jugular ganglia (PNJ) complex is a major sensory gateway through which gustatory, visceral, and somatosensory information from the body is transmitted to the brain. Despite its importance, experimental access to the PNJ complex in mice remains technically challenging, limiting strategies for anatomical tracing and functional manipulation of these pseudounipolar neurons. Here, we detail an improved surgical approach for direct viral vector delivery to the mouse PNJ complex and demonstrate utility of the technique by labeling peripheral and brain-wide central projections from the PNJ. Focusing on the gustatory system, we report viral expression of fluorescent reporters to label gustatory fibers innervating taste tissues at three levels of selectivity: broad labeling of tongue-innervating afferents, genetic targeting of gustatory neurons using P2X2-Cre mice, and selective labeling of sour-responsive neurons using Penk-Cre mice. In the brainstem, the PNJ gustatory neurons terminate at the rostral nucleus of the solitary tract. In addition, we observed PNJ-derived neuron projections to diverse brain regions, including the cervical spinal cord, area postrema, lateral reticular nucleus, nucleus ambiguus, and spinal trigeminal tract. Together, this work provides a practical platform for selectively labeling, isolating, or manipulating PNJ neurons in mice of either sex, enabling future studies of the anatomical organization and functional roles of diverse body-to-brain sensory pathways.Significance Statement The petrosal-nodose-jugular (PNJ) ganglion complex, located in the upper neck, contains sensory neurons that provide critical connections between internal organs and the brain. In this study, we describe an optimized surgical method for directly accessing the PNJ complex and demonstrate its utility by microinjecting viral vectors encoding fluorescent reporters to map sensory neural circuits. As a proof of concept, this approach delineated the tongue-to-brainstem pathway that conveys taste information.

title: The Impact of Injury Severity, Sex, and Nociceptor Activity on Post-Traumatic Temporomandibular Joint Osteoarthritis in Mice.
abstract: Intrinsic and extrinsic trauma to the temporomandibular joint (TMJ) increases the incidence of painful temporomandibular disorders. TMJ trauma also causes increased degeneration of the TMJ structure, leading to TMJ osteoarthritis (TMJOA). Clinically, it is important to identify risk factors of post-traumatic TMJOA, such as sex, injury severity, and persistent post-traumatic pain. We determined the effects of potential risk factors on post-traumatic TMJ degeneration using a mouse model. A repeated forced-mouth opening (FMO) model was used to determine the effect of potential risk factors on post-traumatic TMJOA. Radiographic and histological assays were performed to assess chondral and subchondral degeneration of the TMJ condyles induced by FMO, which was evident after approximately three weeks. To determine the pain-degeneration relationship, we manipulated nociceptor function through chemogenetic inhibition using an inhibitory designer receptor exclusively activated by designer drugs and assessed post-traumatic pain-like behaviours and radiographic and histological changes in TMJ condyles. The extent of post-traumatic TMJ degeneration was greater after 5 days of injury than 2 days. Female mice showed greater post-traumatic TMJ degeneration than males. Chemogenetic silencing of nociceptor activities-only during the period of TMJ injury-inhibited post-traumatic pain-like behaviours but did not prevent the progression of TMJ degeneration. However, chemogenetic silencing of nociceptors throughout the entire traumatic and post-traumatic period did inhibit post-traumatic TMJ degeneration, albeit modestly. Injury severity, sex, and the persistent nociceptor activity modulate the extent of post-traumatic TMJOA.

title: Emergence of Deviance Detection in Cortical Cultures Through Maturation, Criticality, and Early Experience.
abstract: Mismatch negativity (MMN) in humans is widely interpreted as reflecting deviance detection (DD) within predictive processing frameworks. However, the developmental processes by which DD emerges and matures during early cortical development remain incompletely understood. Here, we longitudinally tracked the development of DD in dissociated cortical cultures grown on high-density CMOS microelectrode arrays from Day In Vitro (DIV) 10 to DIV30 (Study 1) and compared cultures with and without early structured stimulation at DIV31-35 (Study 2). Cultures were stimulated with oddball and many-standards control paradigms while spontaneous and evoked activity were recorded. In Study 1, stimulus-evoked responses at early stages were largely confined to fast components corresponding to direct stimulation effects. From DIV15 onward, robust late responses emerged, and deviant stimuli evoked stronger responses than frequent and control stimuli, marking the emergence of DD as defined in this study. By DIV30, responses became stronger, faster, and more temporally precise. Neuronal avalanche analysis revealed a transition from subcritical to near-critical dynamics across development. Cultures exhibiting power-law-like statistics showed larger DD indices, although DD was also observed in non-critical networks. These findings indicate that critical dynamics are not required for DD, but critical-like states are associated with more robust and differentiated DD responses as networks mature. In Study 2, both groups shifted toward power-law-like avalanche distributions, with no significant difference in their developmental trajectories. At DIV31-35, stimulated cultures had earlier peak responses and lower DD indices than controls, but these group differences were not significant. Together, these findings indicate that dissociated cortical cultures can exhibit DD under simplified in vitro conditions and that its developmental trajectory is associated with network maturation and self-organization toward critical-like dynamics.

title: Dysferlin promotes inflammatory macrophage responses and modulates Ca2+-dependent STAT1 signaling.
abstract: Macrophage differentiation and activation shape tissue homeostasis and regeneration. Dysferlin (DYSF) is best known for its role in membrane repair in skeletal muscle, but its function in immune cells remains poorly understood. Here, we identify DYSF as a regulator of inflammatory macrophage-associated activation. DYSF expression increased during monocyte-to-macrophage differentiation. Gain- and loss-of-function analyses revealed that DYSF promoted inflammatory macrophage-associated responses, including cytokine production and migration. DYSF also enhanced Ca2+ influx and STAT1 Ser727-associated signaling, whereas Dysf knockdown or Ca2+ entry inhibition suppressed these responses. DYSF expression increased with aging in human CD14-positive cells and mouse monocyte/macrophage-lineage cells, and DYSF-expressing F4/80-positive macrophage-lineage cells accumulated in aged skeletal muscle. In a macrophage-myoblast co-culture system, DYSF-enriched inflammatory macrophages inhibited myogenic differentiation and myotube fusion, with this effect being partially mediated by soluble inflammatory factors, demonstrating an influence of macrophage DYSF on neighboring myogenic cells in vitro. Together, these findings support a role for DYSF in Ca2+-dependent STAT1-associated inflammatory responses in macrophages and in the suppression of myogenesis in cellular models.

title: The ROCK1 PHC1 domain mediates recruitment to Rho activity zones and contractility signaling.
abstract: The spatiotemporal regulation of cell contraction is crucial for numerous biological processes. In particular, local, subcellular contraction pulses in the cell cortex contribute to mechanotransduction and tissue rearrangements during embryonic development. We previously identified a signaling network that generates mechanosensitive contraction pulses in adherent mammalian cells through positive and negative feedback regulation of the small GTPase RhoA. Here, we show that ROCK1 is rapidly recruited to cortical pulsatile Rho activity zones and that efficient recruitment is synergistically mediated by the canonical Rho-binding domain and the C-terminal PHC1 domain. Surprisingly, the isolated ROCK1 PHC1 domain by itself is already sufficient for dynamic recruitment to active Rho signaling zones in cells, and AlphaFold-guided mutagenesis identifies conserved PHC1 residues that are required for this recruitment. Functional investigations show that the PHC1 domain plays an important role in transduction of Rho activity to myosin activation. Together, our data revise models of ROCK1 regulation by identifying a C-terminal PHC1 domain-dependent mechanism that contributes to ROCK1 recruitment and signal transduction during cell contraction pulses.

title: Autolysosomal enhancer GHF201 attenuates pathophysiology in a mucopolysaccharidosis type I mouse model.
abstract: Mucopolysaccharidosis type I (MPS-I) is a hereditary lysosomal storage disorder caused by deficiency in the lysosomal enzyme α-L-iduronidase (IDUA) leading to pathogenic over-accumulation of glycosaminoglycans (GAGs), major constituent of connective tissue and mediators of cell signaling. We tested the therapeutic efficacy of the autolysosomal activator GHF201 in the Idua -/- mouse model of MPS-I. We show that GHF201 reduced GAGs and increased cathepsin activity in Idua -/- mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) and brain cells. In vivo GHF201 improved aberrant locomotion and behavior, reduced interstitial cathepsins in joints and liver, increased systemic catabolism, corrected bone dysplasia, increased autophagic flux, and ameliorated CNS neurodegeneration and neuroinflammation. GHF201 also reduced brain N-glycans, which are degraded in lysosomes. In conclusion, the lysosomal and autophagic activator GHF201 was demonstrated to improve various pathophysiological parameters in MPS-I-modeling Idua -/- female mice. Our results suggest that GHF201 can complement the inadequate Aldurazyme enzyme replacement therapy as an add-on therapy.

title: [The role of caregivers in crisis day treatment programs for adolescents: Limits in the service of care].
abstract: Program 10-15 is a crisis day hospital for adolescents. Its operations are inspired by institutional psychiatry and the systemic approach. This article describes the use of institutional, educational, and relational boundaries in their role as a source of containment and for therapeutic purposes. Through the presentation of a clinical case study, it illustrates the importance of multidisciplinary teamwork in using boundaries as a therapeutic tool. Opportunities for reflection and sharing within the team are described as necessary to prevent the blurring of professional identities and burnout.

title: [Toward a transitional concept of boundaries in pediatric clinical practice].
abstract: This article proposes a transitional conception of boundaries in order to understand them in terms of their psychological and intersubjective dimensions, rather than solely in terms of their regulatory and rehabilitative functions. To do so, it is essential to recognize that the frameworks and interventions offered to children should be differentiated according to whether they occur in everyday or therapeutic settings, while maintaining a continuity that should not be confused with rigidity. An example drawn from a "Storytelling in the Day Hospital" group will provide an inside look at these essential clinical nuances.

title: [Setting boundaries, establishing a framework].
abstract: The framework is a fundamental aspect of care: it helps give meaning to the therapeutic process. Its contours define a supportive and secure space in which the child can continue or resume his or her development. The infant must construct his or her own sense of self; he or she does so based on the perception of his or her bodily limits, which serve as a container for the psyche and organize a body capable of relating to others and oriented in space. Setting a limit or a prohibition allows the child to encounter another-someone different from themselves-on whom they can rely and who offers them the opportunity to process frustration and reflect on loss. The caregiver is the guardian of the framework, which they must embody and adapt to the child's needs, while respecting the child's otherness.

title: A multi-omics perspective on bipolar disorder.
abstract: Bipolar disorder (BD) is a complex mood disorder with multifactorial biological origins, and omics research has been playing a central role in unraveling its molecular signatures. This chapter provides a descriptive overview of current multi-omics findings in BD, integrating evidence from genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics, lipidomics, and metallomics. Across these omic layers, biological signatures have been proposed, including alterations in neuroinflammatory pathways, mitochondrial and energy-metabolism dysfunction, oxidative stress, neurotransmitter regulation, and lipid signaling. In this chapter, discoveries from each omics domain are summarized and points of intersection that contribute to a broader systems-level view of BD pathophysiology are highlighted. Focusing on the main molecular insights generated over the past decade, this chapter offers a multi-omics narrative that demonstrates how diverse biological processes interact to outline BD clinical features, course, and heterogeneity.

title: Reply to "From environmental to endogenous airway exposures: Rethinking gastroesophageal reflux as more than an asthma comorbidity".

title: Early interventions for primary care patients with stress-related mental ill health: a randomised controlled non-inferiority trial of a nurse-led collaborative care intervention versus cognitive behavioural therapy.
abstract: Stress-related mental ill health is highly prevalent, and most individuals first seek help in primary care where access to psychological support is often limited. To test whether nurse-led collaborative care (CC) is non-inferior to cognitive behavioural therapy delivered as psychologist-guided self-help (GSH-CBT) in reducing stress for adult primary care patients with stress-related mental ill health. A randomised controlled non-inferiority trial where 172 adult primary care patients with mild to moderate stress-related mental ill health were allocated to nurse-led CC or GSH-CBT (1:1). The primary outcome was the Perceived Stress Scale-10 administered every 3 weeks during the 12-week treatment phase. The a priori non-inferiority margin was 0.3 d, requiring the one-sided 95% CI of the effect size to fall within this bound. Secondary outcomes were symptoms of exhaustion, sleep problems, depressive symptoms, general anxiety and quality of life. In both conditions, participants showed large, significant within-group improvements on the primary outcome and all secondary outcomes. The primary outcome showed a small between-group difference (d=0.22), favouring GSH-CBT, with the CI upper bound (0.52) exceeding the non-inferiority margin. For secondary outcomes, GSH-CBT led to a greater reduction in exhaustion (d=0.28; 95% CI 0.64 to 0.002). No other between-group differences were observed. Nurse-led CC was not non-inferior to GSH-CBT. Effect differences were small, but improvements were slightly larger in GSH-CBT. Given that nurse-led CC is safe, easy to administer, and that significant within-group improvements were observed across all measures, this intervention could be a viable option in primary care settings where psychologist-delivered treatment is limited.

title: Lessons from the history of antipsychotic discovery: part 2 - dopaminergic diversification.
abstract: This article examines the development of antipsychotic medications in the period following the discovery of chlorpromazine in the mid-1950s up to the early 21st century. This era is defined by the identification of dopamine modulation as the central mechanism for treating psychosis, and by the development of a diversity of treatments around this mechanism. This strategy yielded a broad range of effective treatments and transformed clinical care; however, with the notable exception of clozapine, it failed to produce substantial gains in overall efficacy. Newer agents primarily differed in tolerability rather than therapeutic impact. Partial dopamine agonists refined, rather than replaced, this approach. As a result, the dopaminergic era offers a cautionary lesson for psychiatric drug development and underscores the need to move beyond dopamine-based models per se.

title: Lessons from the history of antipsychotic discovery: part 1 - initial insights.
abstract: The recent introduction of the first non-dopaminergic antipsychotic marks a pivotal moment in psychopharmacology. This article revisits the development of chlorpromazine, the world's first licensed antipsychotic, and considers what its history reveals about innovation in psychiatric drug discovery. Chlorpromazine emerged in the early 1950s as a treatment for surgical shock. Its subsequent recognition as an antipsychotic transformed psychiatric care, ushering in the modern era of psychopharmacology. This article argues that chlorpromazine's success was not serendipitous: it depended on specific enabling conditions, including rigorous behavioural neuroscience, astute clinical observation across disciplines, close collaboration between clinicians and industry, and relatively agile regulatory frameworks. Understanding these factors is essential as psychiatry enters a new phase of drug development for the treatment of psychosis.

title: Lessons from the history of antipsychotic discovery: part 3 - muscarinic mechanisms.
abstract: After more than seven decades in which antipsychotic drug development has been dominated by dopaminergic mechanisms, the recent emergence of a muscarinic receptor-based treatment represents a conceptual shift in the pharmacotherapy of psychosis. This article reviews the history and development of the first clinically effective non-dopaminergic antipsychotic, tracing its origins to unexpected behavioural effects observed during trials of muscarinic agonists developed for Alzheimer's disease. Early studies of the muscarinic agonist xanomeline demonstrated antipsychotic efficacy, but were limited by poor tolerability due to peripheral cholinergic adverse effects. Subsequent progress depended on the dissociation of central therapeutic effects from peripheral side-effects, through the combination of xanomeline with the peripherally restricted muscarinic antagonist trospium. The development of this treatment highlights several broader lessons for psychiatric drug discovery, including the value of revisiting previously abandoned compounds, the benefits of leveraging existing human safety data on the importance of early-phase translational research and the role of innovative companies.

title: Microbiota-Brain Interactions in Dementia: Role of Diet in Neuroinflammation.
journal: Annals of geriatric medicine and research
abstract: Aging is one of the risk factors for dementia, a group of neurocognitive disorders characterized by a progressive decline in cognitive function. Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the most prevalent, followed by vascular dementia (VaD). Other subtypes, such as frontotemporal dementia (FTD) and Lewy body disease (LBD), are less common but exhibit distinctive symptoms related to motor deficits, behavioral changes, and neuropsychiatric disturbances. Each type of dementia is associated with specific pathological features, such as amyloid plaques in AD and tau tangles in FTD. Recent research highlights the significant role of gut microbiota in the pathogenesis of dementia. Gut dysbiosis, or an imbalance in the gut microbiota, has been linked to neuroinflammation, cognitive decline, and neurodegenerative diseases through the gut-brain axis (GBA). Key microbial species, such as Bacteroides and Firmicutes, produce metabolites that influence neuroinflammation, immune response, and the integrity of the blood-brain barrier (BBB). Short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), such as butyrate, have anti-inflammatory effects, while tryptophan derivatives, such as indole-3-acetic acid (IAA), support intestinal barrier function and modulate neuroinflammatory pathways. Microbial-derived metabolites may serve as potential therapeutic targets to mitigate neurodegeneration, highlighting the intricate relationship between the gut microbiota and brain health. Dietary interventions, such as a balanced diet rich in fiber, antioxidants, and anti-inflammatory compounds, may help support gut health by promoting a balanced gut microbiota and reducing the risk of developing dementia. This review highlights the relationship between brain function, gut microbiota composition, and dementia, providing insights into potential dietary strategies for prevention and management.

title: How vascular territories change in intracranial atherosclerosis - a CT perfusion flow territory mapping study.
journal: Journal of stroke and cerebrovascular diseases : the official journal of National Stroke Association
abstract: Intracranial atherosclerosis is common and has a high recurrence rate. It has been theorized that vascular territory volumes change in ICAD due to collateral activation, but this has not been demonstrated. CT perfusion territory flow mapping is a recently developed technique that uses the collision of wavefronts from perfusion data of different territories to calculate territory volumes. We aimed to investigate how territory volumes change in ICAD. This was a multi-centre international case-control study where we measured arterial territory volumes in 72 patients with ICAD, as well as 49 controls using CT perfusion-based flow territory mapping. ICAD-affected and ICAD-adjacent territory volumes were compared to their homologous pairs and to control patient territories. Correlation between territory volumes and percentage vessel stenosis was tested. The territory volumes in the ICAD-affected regions were significantly smaller (p<0.001) and adjacent territories significantly larger (p<0.001) than homologous contralateral territories. ICAD-affected territory volume ratios were also significantly smaller than control territory ratios, median 0.84 (IQR 0.63-0.99) vs 0.97 (IQR 0.87-1.09), p<0.001. For the largest group (MCA affected territories), the median of the ICAD affected sides was 232.3mls (IQR 162.4-275.9mls) and the median of the unaffected sides was 270.1mls (IQR 241.0-303.7mls). Adjacent territory ratios were significantly larger than control territory ratios 1.19 (IQR 0.95-1.55) vs 0.97 (IQR 0.87-1.09), p<0.001. This study demonstrates that the presence of ICAD is associated with reduction in volume of the affected arterial territory with increases in the adjacent territory volumes.

title: Anterior cingulate cortex glutamatergic projection neurons modulate motion sickness susceptibility via a cortico-vestibular circuit.
abstract: Motion sickness (MS) is a prevalent and debilitating vestibular disorder with limited therapeutic options, yet the cortical mechanisms governing individual susceptibility remain elusive. Using a biaxial rotation mouse model, we investigated the role of the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) in MS by integrating morphology, calcium imaging, electrophysiology, cell ablation, chemogenetics, and optogenetics. Biaxial rotation induced hypothermia, anorexia, taste avoidance, locomotor hypoactivity, and gait incoordination. ACC pyramidal neurons exhibited enhanced activation and increased intrinsic excitability following vestibular stimulation. Ablation of ACC CaMKII+ neurons alleviated MS symptoms, and bidirectional chemogenetic manipulation demonstrated that ACC glutamatergic projection neurons are both necessary and sufficient for MS behaviors. Furthermore, the ACC to medial vestibular nuclei parvicellular part (MVePC) projection was identified as a previously uncharacterized cortico-vestibular circuit that bidirectionally mediates MS susceptibility. Whole-brain projectome analysis further revealed anatomically heterogeneous projection subtypes of ACC-medial vestibular neurons. These findings advance our understanding of the cortical mechanisms underlying MS and establish the ACC-MVePC pathway as a mechanistic entry point for future neuromodulatory strategies.

title: Multi-Level Toxicity of 6PPD-Q and TiO2 Nanoparticles in Mytilus coruscus: Links among Neurochemical, Circadian and Metabolic Responses.
abstract: Tire-derived 6PPD-quinone (6PPD-Q) and titanium dioxide nanoparticles (TiO2 NPs) are increasingly detected in aquatic environments, yet their combined effects on marine bivalves remain poorly understood. In this study, the thick-shell mussel Mytilus coruscus was exposed to 6PPD-Q, TiO2 NPs, and their mixtures to evaluate multi-level physiological, biochemical, histological, and molecular responses. The results demonstrated that 6PPD-Q and TiO2 NPs, particularly under high-concentration co-exposure, significantly impaired mussel physiological performance, as indicated by reduced clearance rate and O:N ratio, increased oxygen consumption and excretion rate, and pronounced gill histopathological injury. Co-exposure also caused clear energy metabolic disruption, including decreased ATP content and inhibited CS, LDH, and PK activities, together with suppressed neurotransmitter levels of DA, ACh, and GABA. In addition, the expression patterns of circadian rhythm- and metabolism-related genes, including CRY, Per2, PPARγ, ACO, and PEPCK, were markedly altered, suggesting disruption of neuro-circadian-metabolic regulation. Oxidative stress was evident in both gills and digestive gland, as reflected by altered CAT and SOD activities and elevated MDA levels. These responses were accompanied by significant modulation of inflammatory and apoptotic genes, including TNF-α, IL-17, TGF-β, Caspase-3, Caspase-8, and Bcl-2. These findings suggest that 6PPD-Q and TiO2 NPs may jointly impair mussel health by linking gill first-contact injury with metabolic dysregulation, oxidative stress, and immune-apoptotic damage.

title: Relational Authority: Religious and Political Iconography in Dialogue with Dermatology.

title: The paraventricular nucleus of the thalamus differentiates threat and safety cues during delayed recall in humans.
abstract: The neural mechanisms supporting delayed threat memory recall in humans remain poorly understood. Animal studies indicate that the paraventricular nucleus of the thalamus (PVT) contributes to threat-memory retrieval after longer retention intervals, but whether the human PVT shows cue-related discriminability during delayed recall remains unclear. Human neuroimaging studies of threat learning have largely focused on memory assessed within 24-48 h, limiting insight into neural responses when previously threatening cues are re-encountered after longer delays. Here, adult participants completed threat acquisition on Day 1 and returned 7-10 days later (n = 28) for a delayed threat-memory recall task while undergoing fMRI. We examined activity in the dorsal midline thalamus centered on a histology-informed PVT region of interest. During Day 1 acquisition, the PVT did not discriminate between CS+ and CS-, despite differential electrodermal activity (EDA) and unconditioned stimulus expectancy ratings. In contrast, during early Day 7 recall, the PVT showed greater activation to previously reinforced CS+ than CS-. In an independent sample (n = 56), PVT activity similarly did not discriminate between CS+ and CS- during acquisition or immediate extinction, but overall PVT activation was greater during acquisition than extinction, regardless of CS type. These findings provide preliminary evidence that a human PVT-centered dorsal midline thalamic region is sensitive to prior threat reinforcement during delayed recall, while also showing engagement during acute threat-learning contexts. More broadly, they support future investigation of PVT-centered thalamic circuitry in the persistence, retrieval, and updating of threat memories, as well as in salience-related processes.

title: Beyond Molecular Snapshots: Regulatory Trajectories in Dynamic Epigenetic Regulation.
abstract: Epigenetic regulation is commonly interpreted through molecular markers measured at discrete timepoints. While such approaches have generated important biological insights, they primarily provide static representations of regulatory states and may therefore capture only a limited component of dynamic biological processes. Emerging evidence from chromatin biology, transcriptional regulation and genome organisation suggests that biological regulation unfolds through continuously evolving interactions across multiple molecular layers. This article presents a biological hypothesis and conceptual framework proposing that epigenetic regulation may be more fully understood through dynamic regulatory trajectories rather than isolated molecular states. The framework conceptualises regulatory states as multidimensional configurations composed of interacting molecular layers and proposes that successive observations form longitudinal trajectories that may contain biologically meaningful information not fully captured by single-timepoint measurements. To formalise this concept, we introduce a set of formal representations describing regulatory states, state transitions and longitudinal regulatory trajectories. These representations are not intended as experimentally validated mathematical laws but as a computational formalisation of the framework's underlying assumptions. The framework therefore generates a testable proposition: in defined biological contexts, trajectory-derived features should provide information beyond that available from the most recent molecular state alone.

title: Tongmai Yizhi Decoction Improves Post-Stroke Cognitive Impairment by Inhibiting Monoamine Oxidase to Reduce Dopamine Metabolism.
abstract: Tongmai Yizhi Decoction (TMYZD), a classic Chinese ethnomedical formula derived from Danggui Shaoyao San and Shenghui Decoction, has long been used for post-stroke amnesia and dementia as it activates blood circulation, tonifies kidney essence, resolves phlegm, and opens cerebral orifices. Its clinical efficacy against post-stroke cognitive impairment (PSCI) is verified, but the underlying pharmacological mechanisms remain unclear. This study aimed to investigate the protective effect of TMYZD against PSCI and verify whether it acts via modulating the dopamine metabolic pathway to elucidate its molecular targets and pharmacological basis. Network pharmacology was applied to predict therapeutic targets, and metabolomics combined with mass spectrometry was used to identify regulated pathways. In vivo, middle cerebral artery occlusion/reperfusion rats were assessed for cognitive function, synaptic ultrastructure, and key target proteins. In vitro, HT22 cells under oxygen-glucose deprivation/reoxygenation with monoamine oxidase-B (MAOB) overexpression were used for target validation. PSCI rats exhibited severe cognitive decline and synaptic structural damage. Monoamine oxidase-A (MAOA) and MAOB were identified as core therapeutic targets. TMYZD significantly regulated the dopamine pathway, upregulated tyrosine hydroxylase and dopamine receptor D2, downregulated MAOA/MAOB, and ameliorated synaptic injury. MAOB overexpression partially abolished the neuroprotective effect of TMYZD, confirming MAOB as a key target. TMYZD improves cognitive function in PSCI by regulating dopamine metabolism, elevating dopamine levels, and enhancing synaptic plasticity, with MAOB as a critical target. These findings provide scientific evidence for the ethnomedical application of TMYZD in PSCI.

title: Neuroprotective Effects of Bauhinia variegata Flower Extract against D-Galactose-Induced Age-Related Cognitive Impairment: Modulation of the Oxidative Stress-endoplasmic reticulum Axis.
abstract: Bauhinia variegata is widely used in traditional medicine for the management of disorders associated with inflammation, oxidative stress, and nervous system dysfunction. The presence of flavonoids and phenolics supports its ethnopharmacological relevance to cognitive impairment, both reported to exert neuroprotective, antioxidant, and cholinesterase-inhibitory activities AIM OF THE STUDY: The present study investigated the neuroprotective potential of B. variegata flower ethanolic extract (BV-EtOH) against D-galactose (D-Gal)-induced age-related cognitive impairment in rats, with emphasis on its anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and anti-tauopathic mechanisms. Chronic D-Gal administration (120 mg/kg) for 8 consecutive weeks induced significant oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, and cognitive impairment, whereas BV-EtOH treatment (50, 100, and 200 mg/kg, p.o., 8 weeks) markedly reversed these alterations. BV-EtOH improved learning and memory by reducing escape latency in the Morris Water Maze by 56.3% and increasing target quadrant time by 48.7% (p < 0.01), while the Object Recognition Test showed a 61.4% rise in discrimination index. Biochemically, BV-EtOH restored GSH levels (74.2%) and reduced MDA (63.5%), alongside significant down regulation of TNF-α (52.8%), IL-1β (47.9%), NF-κB (45.6%), and Endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress mediators GRP78, CHOP, and P-PERK (58-67%) (p < 0.001). Notably, p-Tau expression decreased by 54.1% with concurrent inhibition of GSK-3β, while BDNF and NeuN increased by 2.3- and 2.7-fold, respectively, indicating enhanced neurogenesis and synaptic integrity. UPLC-ESI-MS/MS analysis identified 133 bioactive compounds, mainly flavonoids, phenolic acids, proanthocyanidins, and coumarins, collectively contributing to the extract's multitarget modulation of oxidative, inflammatory, ER stress, and tau phosphorylation pathways. These findings demonstrate that BV-EtOH exerts potent neuroprotective efficacy and holds therapeutic promise for the prevention and management of neuroinflammatory and neurodegenerative disorders.

title: Ethnopharmacological relevance of Aristolochia paucinervis leaf: phytochemical profile and assessment of wound healing, antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties.
abstract: Aristolochia paucinervis Pomel is a perennial Western Mediterranean plant, traditionally used to treat wounds, inflammation, snakebites, skin diseases, cancer, infections, and pain. Despite its extensive use, studies on its phytochemistry, pharmacological properties, and safety remains limited. This study provides the first phytochemical characterisation of A. paucinervis leaf decoction and evaluates its total phenolic content, as well as its antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and wound-healing potential, and safety profile. A decoction from A. paucinervis leaf was prepared according to traditional practices. Its phytochemical profile was characterized by HPLC-PDA-MSn and TLC, quantified using HPLC-PDA, and total phenolic content assessed by Folin-Ciocalteau. Antioxidant potential was assessed using in vitro chemical assays (DPPH, ABTS, and FRAP). Anti-inflammatory activity and safety were preliminary assessed in RAW 264.7 macrophages, by NO and resazurin assays, respectively. Wound-healing potential and safety were determined using the scratch wound assay in NIH/3T3 fibroblasts. HPLC-PDA-MSn analysis revealed caffeoylmalic acid as the major compound, followed by an acetyl-p-coumaroyl hexoside, puerol A, protocatechuic acid hexoside, ferulic acid and isorhamnetin-O-dihexoside. The extract exhibited total phenolic content of 109.59 ± 1.39 mg GAE/g, and demonstrated antioxidant activity across the in vitro chemical assays employed (DPPH, ABTS and FRAP). The decoction evidenced a dose-dependent inhibition of NO production in macrophages (IC50 = 34.99 ± 0.16 μg/mL), without cell-damaging effects. In NIH/3T3 fibroblasts, the extract showed the highest wound closure at 10 μg/mL, whereas both lower and higher concentrations exhibited diminished effects. A. paucinervis leaf decoction results suggested antioxidant, anti-inflammatory and wound-healing activities, without cell-damaging effects, supporting its widespread traditional use in the treatment of skin lesions and underscoring its potential as a future therapeutic drug.

title: LRRC8/VRAC channels at the biophysical interface between cell-volume regulation and context-dependent cell-state transitions.
journal: Progress in biophysics and molecular biology
abstract: Cell volume is a dynamic physical state variable that changes membrane geometry, intracellular ionic strength, macromolecular concentration, molecular surface density, and reaction kinetics. Leucine-rich repeat-containing 8/volume-regulated anion channels (LRRC8/VRACs) provide a molecularly tractable system for testing how these biophysical changes influence cellular behavior. This review critically evaluates evidence linking LRRC8 channel composition, gating, inorganic-anion and organic-solute transport, regulatory volume decrease, and context-dependent cell-state transitions. We distinguish five mechanistic levels: canonical osmotic volume recovery; biophysical signal transduction through volume-dependent preservation of signaling-molecule density or membrane-potential change; transport of signaling metabolites, nucleotides, neurotransmitters, and drugs; channel-associated protein interactions; and tissue-level phenotypes in which the proximal mechanism remains unresolved. Activated mouse T-cells provide a clear mechanistic example: LRRC8A supports blast formation under weak stimulation, with signaling-density preservation tested using acute hypotonic swelling. In other settings, LRRC8 subunit composition modifies cyclic GMP-AMP, ATP, glutamate, taurine, glutathione, and platinum-drug transport, producing lineage-, stimulus-, and cargo-specific outcomes. Studies in nervous, immune, metabolic, vascular, epithelial, reproductive, and malignant tissues reveal substantial biological breadth but also expose recurring interpretive limitations, including incomplete definition of native channel stoichiometry, reliance on nonspecific inhibitors, inadequate separation of conductance from scaffolding, and failure to measure volume, substrate flux, signaling, and phenotype within the same causal sequence. We synthesize conflicting findings, identify model-dependent explanations, and propose experimental standards based on subunit-resolved rescue, pore-mutants, orthogonal-mechanical and osmotic perturbations, compartment-specific flux measurements, and time-resolved single-cell analysis. Current evidence supports LRRC8/VRAC as a family of context-dependent biophysical and metabolic gates rather than a universal cell-fate switch.

title: Changes in Weight and Metabolic Indices after Switching to Aripiprazole Once-Monthly in Patients with Schizophrenia According to Prior Oral Antipsychotics.
abstract: Antipsychotic-induced weight gain and metabolic disturbance are common in schizophrenia, but liability varies across agents. Aripiprazole has a relatively favorable metabolic profile, yet evidence on aripiprazole once-monthly, its long-acting injectable formulation, remains limited. We hypothesized that switching from a higher liability antipsychotic would yield a greater weight reduction than switching from a lower liability agent. This 16-week, prospective, open-label, multicenter study enrolled patients with stable schizophrenia. Participants were stratified by the metabolic liability of their prior oral antipsychotic (high vs. low). Participants received aripiprazole once-monthly 400 mg intramuscularly every 4 weeks, with cross-titration of the prior agent. Anthropometric and metabolic parameters were assessed every 4 weeks from baseline. Weight changes at week 16 were the principal outcome, and all analyses were exploratory. Mixed models for repeated measures evaluated changes over time, adjusting for covariates. Among the 151 participants (100 low-risk and 51 high-risk participants), weight, body mass index, and waist circumference decreased significantly in the high-risk group only, and more high-risk patients reached clinically meaningful improvement. Most lipid and glycemic indices changed little, although low-density lipoprotein cholesterol and total cholesterol decreased in both groups. Psychiatric symptoms remained stable. In a subgroup switched from oral aripiprazole (n=73), anthropometric and metabolic parameters were all unchanged. In patients previously exposed to high-metabolic-risk antipsychotics, switching to aripiprazole once-monthly was associated with short-term reductions in weight and central adiposity-consistent with the reversal of the prior agents' metabolic burden-while psychiatric stability was maintained. Longer-term studies are needed to confirm their durability and clinical significance.

title: Left or right - the development of handedness and its significance in everyday hand surgery.
journal: Handchirurgie, Mikrochirurgie, plastische Chirurgie : Organ der Deutschsprachigen Arbeitsgemeinschaft fur Handchirurgie : Organ der Deutschsprachigen Arbeitsgemeinschaft fur Mikrochirurgie der Peripheren Nerven und Gefasse : Organ der V...
abstract: Handedness describes the preference for using one hand over the other in fine and gross motor tasks and represents a key manifestation of functional brain asymmetry. Around 90% of the world's population is right-handed. The development of handedness is based on a complex interplay of genetic, epigenetic, neurobiological, developmental psychological and environmental factors. Prenatal movement patterns allow conclusions to be drawn about future handedness at an early stage. However, genetic influences explain only part of the variance, meaning that polygenic and regulatory mechanisms, as well as perinatal and postnatal influences, contribute significantly to the development and stabilisation of handedness. Handedness has considerable clinical relevance for hand surgery. Injuries to the dominant hand frequently lead to greater subjective limitations, longer rehabilitation and a greater impairment of work capacity and quality of life. At the same time, cortical plasticity offers the possibility for adaptive processes. Taking handedness into account therefore influences the assessment of severity, the choice of treatment strategies, the definition of rehabilitation goals, and the interpretation of patient-reported outcomes. Occupational health aspects are also relevant, as left-handed individuals in right-handed-dominated environments have an increased risk of certain strain and compression syndromes. Furthermore, handedness is relevant not only in patients but also in surgeons, for example with regard to instrumentation, training conditions and bimanual coordination. The aim of this review is to bring together the neurobiological and developmental foundations of handedness and to critically examine their significance for diagnosis, treatment planning, rehabilitation and clinical decision-making processes in hand surgery. An integrative understanding of handedness can help to differentiate treatment strategies more functionally and to optimise them in a patient-centred and scientifically sound manner.

title: Spatial Lipidomics and Transcriptomics Reveal Nicotine-Mediated Restoration of Lipid Homeostasis in Parkinson's Disease.
abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is characterized by progressive dopaminergic neurodegeneration, and increasing evidence implicates disrupted lipid metabolism as a critical contributor to disease pathogenesis. Although nicotine has been associated with a reduced risk of PD, the mechanisms underlying its neuroprotective effects remain incompletely understood. Here, we investigated whether nicotine protects against PD by modulating brain lipid metabolism. Using 1-Methyl-4-phenyl-1,2,3,6-tetrahydropyridine (MPTP)-induced mouse model of PD, we combined behavioral assessments, transcriptomic profiling, and desorption electrospray ionization mass spectrometry imaging to examine the effects of nicotine on motor function, gene expression, and spatial lipid distribution in the brain. Nicotine treatment significantly improved motor performance preserved nigrostriatal dopaminergic neurons, and attenuated neuroinflammatory responses. Spatial lipidomic analysis revealed widespread disturbances in lipid composition within the substantia nigra, striatum, and hippocampus of PD mice, many of which were reversed by nicotine administration. Integrated analysis of transcriptomic and lipidomic data further demonstrated that nicotine reshapes lipid metabolic pathways associated with neuronal survival and inflammatory regulation, leading to restoration of brain lipid homeostasis. Together, these findings provide multimodal evidence that restoration of lipid homeostasis is a key mechanism underlying nicotine-mediated neuroprotection in PD. Our results identify lipid remodeling as a mechanistic link between nicotine exposure and neuroprotection and highlight brain lipid metabolism as a potential therapeutic target for Parkinson's disease.

title: Colonoscopy quality indicators among nurse endoscopists and physicians in population-based colorectal cancer screening in Sweden.
abstract: BACKGROUND : In Sweden, a nationwide colorectal cancer (CRC) screening program for individuals aged 60-74 started in 2021; to meet the increasing demand for colonoscopy, nurse endoscopists may play a key role - provided they maintain high technical quality. This observational study aimed to evaluate the nurse endoscopists' performance in the screening program, focusing on core quality indicators. METHODS : Data were extracted from the Swedish Quality Register for Colonoscopies and Colorectal Cancer Screening (SveReKKS), including all screening colonoscopies performed between 1 April 2019 and 31 August 2025. Key quality indicators - adenoma detection rate (ADR), cecal and ileal intubation rates, bowel preparation, sedation use, and complications - were compared between nurse and physician endoscopists using generalized linear mixed-effects models with a logit link. RESULTS : Of 27 978 colonoscopies, 42 % were performed by nurses. Nurses had a higher ADR (57 % vs. 46 %; odds ratio [OR] 1.55, 95 %CI 1.47-1.62), and 3.6 % of the nurses had an ADR < 25 %, compared with 11.2 % of the physicians. Nurses also had higher odds of ileal intubation (OR 1.2, 95 %CI 1.1-1.2) and longer withdrawal times. CONCLUSIONS : Nurse endoscopists demonstrated high quality colonoscopy performance in CRC screening and represent a valuable resource to meet increasing service demands without compromising clinical standards.

title: Glibenclamide treatment improved intraspinal blood volume, tissue sparing, and functional recovery after cervical spinal cord injury in rats.
abstract: Limiting the expansion of the primary injury after a traumatic spinal cord injury (SCI) can offer improved functional outcomes. Glibenclamide (glyburide) has been shown to limit intraspinal bleeding and promote vascular stability after SCI in rats, but its impact on intraspinal hemodynamics has not been investigated. Here, we hypothesized that acute glibenclamide treatment would improve intraspinal hemodynamics after a cervical contusion SCI in a rat model (200 kdyn). Intravital ultrafast contrast enhanced ultrasound (CEUS) imaging revealed that glibenclamide treatment significantly increased total blood volume (i.e., tissue perfusion) at 72-hours post-injury (hpi) compared to vehicle treated controls (p1.2). Histological data confirmed that glibenclamide treatment significantly lowered caspase-8-positive cells in the white matter at 72-hpi (p1.2). Weekly forelimb locomotor scoring revealed significant functional improvements in animals treated with glibenclamide at 4-weeks post injury (wpi) (p1.2), which continued through to 8-wpi compared to vehicle treated animals (p1.2). Glibenclamide intervention significantly reduced lesion size by 8-wpi compared to controls (p1.2). This study is the first to report in vivo improvements in intraspinal blood volume associated with glibenclamide treatment after acute cervical SCI in rats.

title: Resting-state functional connectivity alterations and neurodevelopmental outcomes in neonates at high risk of hypoxic-ischemic brain injury.
abstract: High risk of hypoxic-ischemic brain injury during the neonatal period may disrupt early brain maturation, yet its impact on large-scale functional network organization and later neurodevelopment remains insufficiently understood. Resting-state functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) was used to characterize cortical functional connectivity in neonates at high risk of hypoxic-ischemic brain injury and controls. Functional connectivity, multivariate pattern analysis, and graph-theoretical approaches were applied to examine group differences in network organization and their associations with developmental outcome. Compared with controls, high-risk neonates showed reduced functional connectivity predominantly within the frontoparietal network. Seed-based multivariate pattern analysis identified the left parietal lobe as the strongest discriminator between groups. Within the frontoparietal subnetwork, the high-risk group showed reduced clustering coefficient and increased global efficiency, suggesting reduced local segregation and atypical network reorganization. Clustering coefficient was positively associated with later Ages and Stages Questionnaire (ASQ-3) scores in both groups, consistent with a general developmental relationship. In contrast, higher global efficiency and lower nodal clustering in the left prefrontal cortex were associated with poorer developmental outcomes only in the high-risk group. Neonates at high risk of hypoxic-ischemic brain injury show early alterations in frontoparietal functional organization, some of which are associated with later neurodevelopment. Resting-state fNIRS-derived connectomic measures may therefore have potential for early risk characterization, although further validation in larger independent cohorts is needed.

title: Integrated multi-omics analyses decipher molecular subtype-associated tumor microenvironment patterns in glioma.
abstract: Glioma progression is driven by both tumor-intrinsic genetics and tumor microenvironment (TME) heterogeneity. Although tumor-intrinsic heterogeneity has been widely explored, the understanding of the isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH)-associated TME in glioma remains less clear. In this study, therefore, we integrated bulk and single-cell transcriptomics, spatial transcriptomics, and proteomic data from glioma tissues and patient blood samples to characterize TME composition, subtype-associated molecular patterns, and their prognostic relevance. The data showed that IDH-wildtype (IDH-WT) glioma exhibited complicated TME, enriched in pericytes and immune cells, whereas IDH-mutant (IDH-MU) glioma displayed a TME dominated by oligodendrocytes and neurons. From a TME-related geneset, we identified four subtype-associated gene patterns: 179 genes in IDH-WT (WT-179) associated with extracellular matrix remodeling and angiogenesis; 68 genes in IDH-MU (MU-68) linked to neuronal and synaptic pathways; 30 genes in IDH-MU with chromosome 1p/19q-non-codeletion (M-N-30) enriched in RNA/protein binding; and 83 genes in IDH-MU with chromosome 1p/19q-codeletion (M-C-83) involved in neurodevelopmental processes. Single-cell transcriptomics profiled contributions of pericyte, myeloid, and lymphocyte subpopulations to these patterns, revealing distinct developmental trajectories and functional programs across glioma subtypes. Glioma tissue and serum proteomics detected WT-179-associated proteins and identified POSTN, LTF, PLA2G2A, and ANXA1 as candidate protein markers associated with the IDH-WT TME program. Taken together, this study provided novel insights into the cellular and molecular features of the TME across glioma molecular subtypes and implied TME as a promising therapeutic target for developing novel treatment strategies.

title: VPS13A loss of function mutations cause disruption of cellular calcium homeostasis and increase the vulnerability to ferroptosis.
abstract: VPS13A belongs to the family of bridge-like lipid transfer proteins, which connect opposing membranes at organelle contact sites in order to facilitate bulk lipid transfer. Loss of function mutations in the VPS13A gene cause VPS13A disease. Diminished store operated calcium entry has previously been described in patient-derived fibroblasts and iPSC-derived neurons from VPS13A disease patients and impairments in mitochondrial calcium uptake was observed in patient-derived fibroblasts. However, how calcium (dys)homeostasis is regulated and its effects on neuronal survival remain enigmatic. Here, we investigated calcium regulation and cell death in induced pluripotent stem cell-derived neurons from VPS13A disease patients. We demonstrate that reduced store operated calcium entry is associated with diminished plasma membrane-ER contact sites and altered expression of the calcium release-activated calcium channel ORAI1. VPS13A-deficient neurons further exhibited elevated mitochondrial calcium levels, as well as resistance of the mitochondrial calcium uniporter to inhibition by Ru360. Further, VPS13A disease neurons show increased lipid peroxidation, driving ferroptotic cell death. These findings establish a mechanistic link between disrupted calcium homeostasis and neuronal degeneration in VPS13A disease and identify calcium (dys)homeostasis and ferroptosis as potential pathogenic pathways and therapeutic targets.

title: From drug repurposing to antiviral activity expansion: building antiviral maps from multiple viral trees.
abstract: We propose an evidence-weighted atlas for drug repurposing and antiviral activity expansion. Instead of using a universal viral phylogeny, our framework matches the way in which viruses are represented to the pharmacological question being asked. The atlas integrates five distinct layers: closely related viruses are represented in whole-genome trees, homologous drug targets in target-specific polymerase or protease trees, deeply diverged virion proteins in structure-derived trees, convergent cellular vulnerabilities in host-dependency networks, and a complementary view of chemical space, linking scaffold variation to breadth, potency and resistance liability, in antiviral structure-activity relationship trees. Candidate drug or activity transfers are filtered by pocket conservation, intracellular activation, tissue exposure, safety and resistance barriers. Successful and failed combinations calibrate the framework, which prioritizes the smallest justified 2-4-agent regimen for untreated viruses and Pathogen X.

title: Lambda-Cyhalothrin Impairs Learning and Memory in Zebrafish by Disrupting Brain Energy Metabolism Coupled to Neurotransmitter Homeostasis via α-Ketoglutarate Depletion.
abstract: Lambda-cyhalothrin (LCT) is a widely used type II pyrethroid insecticide commonly found in global aquatic environments. However, how it impairs cognitive function in non-target aquatic organisms at environmentally relevant concentrations remains poorly understood. In this study, adult zebrafish were chronically exposed to LCT at 0.1, 0.2, and 0.4 μg/L for 28 days. Behavioral tests, histopathological observations, multi-omics, and biochemical analyses were combined to explore the underlying neurotoxic mechanisms. Our results showed that exposure to 0.4 μg/L LCT significantly impaired spatial learning and memory in zebrafish and caused marked neuronal damage along with disrupted mitochondrial ultrastructure in the brain. LCT markedly inhibited key rate-limiting enzymes of glycolysis and the TCA cycle and blocked mitochondrial respiratory chain function, leading to insufficient ATP production and excessive ROS accumulation. Multi-omics integration revealed a severe depletion of cerebral α-ketoglutarate (α-KG) alongside inhibited α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase (α-KGDH) activity and downregulated ogdh transcription. Critically, dietary supplementation with the cell-permeable α-KG analog dimethyl α-ketoglutarate (DM-KG) during LCT exposure restored brain α-KG levels, rescued TCA cycle flux and ATP production, attenuated oxidative stress, and recovered glutamate and GABA contents. These rescue experiments provide direct evidence that α-KG depletion is a key metabolic driver of LCT-induced disruption of energy metabolism and neurotransmitter homeostasis. While behavioral recovery was not assessed in the rescue experiment, these findings establish α-KG as a critical metabolic node in LCT neurotoxicity and offer a potential target for mitigating pyrethroid-induced neurological damage.

title: FGFR-Altered Urothelial Carcinoma in the EV-Pembrolizumab Era: Rationale and Emerging Data for Upfront Triplet Strategies.
abstract: Urothelial cancer (UC) is a common malignancy with a significant incidence worldwide, particularly in Europe and North America. Approximately 5% of patients have de novo metastatic disease at the time of initial diagnosis. The combination of Enfortumab vedotin and Pembrolizumab recently transformed the first-line treatment landscape, providing better clinical outcomes and greater tolerability compared to traditional cisplatin-based therapies. However, alterations in fibroblast growth factor receptor (FGFR) signaling may diminish the effectiveness of Immune Checkpoint Inhibitors (ICIs), underscoring the need for novel combination therapies. This review examines emerging evidence supporting combination strategies incorporating pan-FGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors in FGFR-altered urothelial carcinoma, focusing on their potential integration with first-line doublet regimens. Ongoing and future clinical studies will be essential to define the clinical value of these combinations and to advance precision immunotherapy strategies guided by genomic alterations, to improve outcomes for patients with UC.

title: Chronic Methyl tert-butyl ether exposure disrupts neurodevelopment and selectively impairs dopaminergic neurons.
abstract: Methyl tert-butyl ether (MTBE) is a widely detected environmental contaminant, especially in the water; however, its impact on brain development remains poorly defined. Here, we show that chronic exposure to MTBE (15mg/mL in drinking water) beginning during embryonic development (E9.5) and continuing post-weaning for 18 weeks disrupts neuronal homeostasis and induces long-lasting alterations in dopaminergic neurons and behavior in C57BL/6J mice. In primary neuronal cultures, MTBE suppresses neuronal proliferation, increases apoptotic cell death, and impairs neurite outgrowth, indicating direct neurodevelopmental toxicity. In vivo, MTBE exposure resulted in a reduction of tyrosine hydroxylase-positive dopaminergic neurons, with preferential vulnerability in the ventral tegmental area. Notably, MTBE exposure was associated with increased amyloid precursor protein/β-amyloid-related pathology, suggesting involvement of molecular pathways linked to neurodegeneration. MTBE-exposed mice exhibited consistent motor impairments across multiple behavioral paradigms. Taken together, the results in this study identify MTBE as a developmental neurotoxicant that selectively compromises dopaminergic systems and establishes long-term neurological vulnerability. Therefore, it provides a potential link between environmental exposure and neurodegeneration-related processes.

title: Hyaluronic acid-based CeO₂ nanozymes for brain-targeted Parkinson's disease therapy: Biointerface design, multifunctional neuroprotective regulation and future perspectives: A review.
abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder driven by oxidative imbalance, mitochondrial dysfunction, and persistent neuroinflammation, yet current pharmacological interventions provide symptomatic relief but fail to halt neuronal degeneration largely owing to complex pathological mechanisms and poor blood-brain barrier (BBB) penetration. Cerium oxide (CeO₂) nanozymes have garnered considerable attention for their reversible Ce3+/Ce4+ redox cycling and intrinsic superoxide dismutase (SOD) and catalase (CAT)-like activities, although therapeutic efficacy is restricted by insufficient brain accumulation and limited nano-bio interface interactions. Hyaluronic acid (HA), a naturally occurring polysaccharide, has emerged as a bioactive macromolecule for nano-bio interface engineering, enhancing colloidal stability, biological recognition, cellular uptake, and brain-targeting efficiency of CeO₂ nanozymes via cluster of differentiation 44 (CD44)-mediated targeting of activated microglia. This review systematically summarizes recent advances in HA-CeO₂ nanozyme platforms for PD therapy, with key findings indicating multifaceted neuroprotection through modulation of oxidative stress (Nrf2/ARE), mitochondrial dysfunction (PINK1/Parkin), neuroinflammation (NF-κB/NLRP3), α-synuclein pathology (autophagy-lysosomal pathways), and ferroptosis (Nrf2/SLC7A11/GPX4). Structure-activity relationship analyses reveal that CeO₂ core properties and HA characteristics collectively determine catalytic activity and targeting efficiency. Significant limitations persist, including insufficient structural-efficacy correlations, unclear long-term biosafety, and lack of standardized protocols. By highlighting HA as a bioactive polysaccharide that governs nano-bio interface regulation, this review provides a biomacromolecule-oriented perspective for designing brain-targeted CeO₂ nanozyme platforms, while critically examining the translational barriers that must be overcome to realize their clinical potential.

title: Interactive effect of childhood adversity and HPA-axis multilocus genetic variation on alexithymia in adolescents.
abstract: Childhood adversity increases risk for affective symptoms, including alexithymia, a transdiagnostic emotion-processing difficulty common in adolescence. Hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis-related genetic variation may contribute to individual differences in sensitivity to adverse environments. This study examined whether an HPA-axis-related multilocus genetic profile score (MGPS) moderated the association between childhood adversity and adolescent alexithymia. The present study addressed this issue in a sample of 460 adolescents (Mage = 12.73, SD = 0.72; 54.1% female) who completed the Childhood Trauma Questionnaire and the Toronto Alexithymia Scale. Saliva samples were collected for deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) genotyping, and an HPA-axis-related multilocus genetic profile score (MGPS) was constructed from six candidate polymorphisms. Hierarchical regression and re-parameterized regression analyses were conducted. Childhood adversity was positively associated with alexithymia. HPA-axis MGPS moderated this association. Specifically, adolescents with high HPA-axis MGPS exhibited higher levels of alexithymia when exposed to high childhood adversity but lower levels when exposed to low childhood adversity, providing preliminary support for the differential susceptibility model. The cross-sectional design precludes causal inference, and the findings require replication in longitudinal, clinically enriched, and more diverse samples. HPA-axis multilocus genetic variation may function as a biological sensitivity factor in the association between childhood adversity and adolescent alexithymia. These findings extend gene-environment interaction research to alexithymia and highlight individual differences in adolescents' emotional responses to adversity.

title: Lithium during maintenance electroconvulsive therapy: Secondary neuropsychological outcomes from the open-label PRASED randomized controlled trial.
abstract: Lithium is commonly used for relapse prevention after successful electroconvulsive therapy (ECT). However, the combination of lithium and ECT has warranted caution in clinical practice due to concerns about cognitive tolerability, while evidence remains inconclusive. To evaluate the neuropsychological effects of maintenance ECT (M-ECT), with and without lithium, in patients with major depressive disorder (MDD) across all ages. The Preventing Relapse After Successful Electroconvulsive therapy for Depression (PRASED) study was a multicenter, open-label, randomized controlled trial. Patients who achieved remission after an acute ECT course for MDD were randomized to receive symptom driven M-ECT and maintenance pharmacotherapy with or without adjunctive lithium. In this secondary outcome analysis, neuropsychological functioning was assessed repeatedly over six months using a comprehensive test battery covering global cognition, memory, attention, fluency, processing speed and subjective memory complaints. Linear mixed-effects models were applied to examine group differences in cognitive trajectories over time and associations between serum lithium levels and cognitive outcomes. No significant differences in cognitive trajectories were observed between the lithium (n = 50) and non‑lithium (n = 46) group. Neuropsychological performance improved over time in both groups across all cognitive domains except verbal fluency. Serum lithium levels were not associated with neuropsychological performance. Lithium addition during M-ECT was not associated with impaired objective or subjective neuropsychological functioning. These findings support the neuropsychological tolerability of concurrent lithium and ECT use in the maintenance phase and may help guide treatment decisions regarding relapse prevention following successful ECT.

title: Mapping reproducible brain-based depression stratification across clinical, cognitive, and neurotransmitter dimensions.
abstract: Identifying reproducible brain-based stratifications across independent cohorts is critical for parsing heterogeneity in Major Depressive Disorder (MDD), yet robust profiles spanning micro- and macroscales remain poorly defined. We applied stability-based clustering to cortical thickness (CT) data from 1531 MDD individuals in UK Biobank (UKB), with replication in 144 inpatients from IRCCS San Raffaele Hospital (HSR). Two stable clusters emerged (normalized stability = 0.125) that generalized to a hold-out UKB sample with 96.5% accuracy (majority-cluster baseline = 59.5%). The clusters differed in widespread CT, largely reflected in global CT, with one showing cortical thinning, childhood trauma, and diabetes comorbidity. A two-cluster structure was independently replicated in HSR (normalized stability = 0.29), with a broadly similar cortical topography, although systematic CT differences between cohorts limited direct cross-cohort comparability. The clinical correlates identified in UKB did not replicate after correction for multiple comparisons. In UKB, mapping the CT differences between strata onto Neurosynth meta-analytic activation patterns revealed a ventral-dorsal gradient linked with emotion regulation, interoceptive, and motivational processes. Spatial correlations with 19 neurotransmitter receptors and transporters obtained from positron emission tomography identified the dopamine transporter as the dominant contributor in UKB, and the histamine H3 receptor in HSR. These findings provide a reproducible framework linking CT-based clusters in MDD to multiscale biological organization, although their clinical relevance warrants further investigation.

title: Progression of White Matter Hyperintensities in Older Adults: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
abstract: White matter hyperintensities (WMH) are ubiquitous on magnetic resonance images (MRI) in older adults. However, the rate and mechanisms of their proliferation remain unclear, as they are inferred mainly from cross-sectional studies and imperfect single indicators of theoretical constructs. To assess the magnitude of WMH change and its modifiers, we conducted a meta-analysis of 54 longitudinal studies. We found the increase in WMH burden over time (pooled effect size) even in the studies with rigorous participant health screening. WMH proliferation was faster in the samples with higher mean age but independent of sample's sex or ethno-racial composition. Higher prevalence of vascular disease in the sample and lower sample average of diastolic or mean arterial pressure at baseline yielded faster mean WMH progression. Lower baseline cognitive status in samples with healthiest participants was associated with faster WMH increase. Automatic and manual methods produced equivalent results, but manual intervention in automatic methods yielded higher estimates. We found no evidence of publication bias. To better quantify the WMH progression and the influence of moderators in future studies, we recommend increasing the number of assessment occasions, applying uniform protocols and instruments, using multiple indicators of risk factors and cognitive outcomes, adding assessment of metabolic, energetic, and hemodynamic properties of the brain, applying state-of-the-art statistical modeling methods, providing comprehensive sample descriptions, and reporting the results in greater detail.

title: Spinal cord stimulation in the treatment of chronic pain: from evidence to clinical practice - part 1.
abstract: Neuropathic pain is caused by a lesion or disease of the somatosensory nervous system. Pharmacotherapy remains the primary treatment for this condition, although non-pharmacological modalities such as physical and psychological therapy are also recommended. Due to the limited efficacy of conventional therapies, interventional modalities such as spinal cord stimulation (SCS) are increasingly used. Several theories have been formulated to explain the analgesic mechanism of SCS. These include the gate control theory, neurochemical and immunological mechanisms, synaptic plasticity, and cortical reorganization. Clinical data were analyzed in a systematic review of the literature that identified eight systematic reviews with meta-analyses. Most of the meta-analyses indicate that SCS provides statistically superior outcomes compared with conventional therapy or placebo in terms of pain intensity, degree of disability, and quality of life. Safety was evaluated in one systematic review, in which the estimated risks of lead or wire displacement/breakage and infection were significantly higher in the SCS arm than in the conventional therapy arm. The benefits of earlier implementation of SCS in the therapeutic regimen are becoming recognized. It is necessary to clearly define the role of SCS in the multidisciplinary treatment of patients with neuropathic pain.

title: The Gut-Brain Axis in Parkinson's Disease: From Clinical Observation toward Mechanism-Based Precision Medicine.
journal: Movement disorders : official journal of the Movement Disorder Society
abstract: Gastrointestinal dysfunction is increasingly recognized as a core feature of Parkinson's disease (PD), affecting quality of life, nutrition, medication response, and potentially the earliest stages of pathogenesis. This perspective traces the evolution of the gut from a neglected source of non-motor symptoms to a central component of biological models of PD. Gastrointestinal manifestations are physiologically heterogeneous and require objective phenotyping to distinguish dysphagia, gastroparesis, slow transit, defecatory dysfunction, and overlapping mechanisms. The body-first/brain-first framework further suggests that Lewy pathology may follow distinct anatomical trajectories, with early enteric and autonomic involvement defining a subgroup in which gut-directed biomarkers and therapies may be especially relevant. Alterations of the gut microbiome are reproducibly associated with PD, although geography, constipation, medication, diet, disease stage, and reverse causation complicate interpretation. Emerging work is shifting from taxonomy toward microbial functions and host pathways, including barrier integrity, immune and enteroendocrine signaling, short-chain fatty acids, glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1), host genetic susceptibility, α-synuclein aggregation and propagation, and microbial levodopa metabolism. Trials of probiotics, fecal microbiota transplantation, and dietary interventions remain heterogeneous and have not established disease-modifying efficacy. Progress will require longitudinal studies in prodromal and subtype-defined populations, objective gastrointestinal measurements, integrated microbial, host-genetic and other multi-omics, mechanistic human and animal models, and clinical trials combining target-engagement markers with meaningful outcomes. Such an approach may enable precision gut-brain medicine for appropriately selected patients with PD. © 2026 The Author(s).
